question.question_text: A blog needs good SEO and fast first content, but its admin dashboard sits behind login and is highly interactive. Which approach fits best?
question.question_html: A blog needs good SEO and fast first content, but its admin dashboard sits behind login and is highly interactive. Which approach fits best?

options.label: A
options.text: SSR for public pages, CSR for the dashboard

options.label: B
options.text: CSR everywhere, plus a sitemap for crawlers

options.label: C
options.text: SSR everywhere, with no client JavaScript

options.label: D
options.text: CSR for public pages, SSR for the dashboard

question.explanation: Public pages need SEO and a fast first paint, which SSR gives. The dashboard is behind login, so it needs no SEO, and its heavy interactivity suits CSR.

question.question_text: User 7 is stored with name, email and phone. A client sends PUT /users/7 with body {"name": "Asha"}. Under strict PUT semantics, what is stored afterwards?
question.question_html: User 7 is stored with name, email and phone. A client sends PUT /users/7 with body {"name": "Asha"}. Under strict PUT semantics, what is stored afterwards?

options.label: A
options.text: Name updated; email and phone unchanged

options.label: B
options.text: A new user 8 created with name Asha

options.label: C
options.text: Only name remains; email and phone gone

options.label: D
options.text: Rejected, since PUT needs the id in body

question.explanation: PUT replaces the whole resource with the body sent, so fields left out are removed. A partial update is what PATCH is for.

question.question_text: Which pair of methods is idempotent but not safe?
question.question_html: Which pair of methods is idempotent but not safe?

options.label: A
options.text: GET and HEAD

options.label: B
options.text: PUT and DELETE

options.label: C
options.text: POST and PATCH

options.label: D
options.text: GET and DELETE

question.explanation: Repeating PUT or DELETE leaves the server in the same state, so both are idempotent. Both change data, so neither is safe. GET and HEAD are safe and idempotent.

question.question_text: A logged-in regular user calls DELETE /admin/users/5. The token is valid, but the user has no admin rights. Which status code fits?
question.question_html: A logged-in regular user calls DELETE /admin/users/5. The token is valid, but the user has no admin rights. Which status code fits?

options.label: A
options.text: 401 Unauthorized

options.label: B
options.text: 400 Bad Request

options.label: C
options.text: 404 Not Found

options.label: D
options.text: 403 Forbidden

question.explanation: The user is authenticated, since the token is valid, but lacks permission, so 403. 401 would mean the user is not logged in.

question.question_text: A client sends a JSON body with Content-Type: text/plain to an endpoint that only accepts application/json. Which status code fits?
question.question_html: A client sends a JSON body with Content-Type: text/plain to an endpoint that only accepts application/json. Which status code fits?

options.label: A
options.text: 406 Not Acceptable

options.label: B
options.text: 400 Bad Request

options.label: C
options.text: 415 Unsupported Media Type

options.label: D
options.text: 422 Unprocessable Content

question.explanation: 415 means the server can't accept the request body's Content-Type. 406 is about the Accept header, the format the client wants back.

question.question_text: A server sends Set-Cookie: sid=abc; Max-Age=3600; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax. Which statement is true?
question.question_html: A server sends Set-Cookie: sid=abc; Max-Age=3600; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax. Which statement is true?

options.label: A
options.text: The browser sends it only over HTTPS

options.label: B
options.text: It is deleted when the tab is closed

options.label: C
options.text: Page scripts can read it from document.cookie

options.label: D
options.text: It is sent on every cross-site POST request

question.explanation: Secure means the cookie travels only over HTTPS. HttpOnly blocks scripts, SameSite=Lax blocks cross-site POSTs, and Max-Age keeps it for an hour even after the tab closes.

question.question_text: old-shop.com has moved for good to new-shop.com. Which response keeps the search ranking?
question.question_html: old-shop.com has moved for good to new-shop.com. Which response keeps the search ranking?

options.label: A
options.text: 302 with a Location header

options.label: B
options.text: 200 with a meta refresh tag

options.label: C
options.text: 307 with a Location header

options.label: D
options.text: 301 with a Location header

question.explanation: 301 is a permanent redirect, so search engines move the ranking to the new URL. 302 and 307 are temporary redirects.

question.question_text: For a first visit to https://api.app.com/orders, which order of steps is correct?
question.question_html: For a first visit to https://api.app.com/orders, which order of steps is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: TCP connection → DNS lookup → TLS handshake → HTTP request

options.label: B
options.text: DNS lookup → TCP connection → TLS handshake → HTTP request

options.label: C
options.text: DNS lookup → TLS handshake → TCP connection → HTTP request

options.label: D
options.text: TLS handshake → DNS lookup → TCP connection → HTTP request

question.explanation: DNS first finds the IP, then a TCP connection opens, then TLS is set up on top of it. Only then is the HTTP request sent.

question.question_text: Nginx forwards a request to a Node server that has crashed, and the connection is refused. What does the client most likely get from Nginx?
question.question_html: Nginx forwards a request to a Node server that has crashed, and the connection is refused. What does the client most likely get from Nginx?

options.label: A
options.text: 500 Internal Server Error

options.label: B
options.text: 504 Gateway Timeout

options.label: C
options.text: 502 Bad Gateway

options.label: D
options.text: 503 Service Unavailable

question.explanation: 502 means the gateway got no valid response from the upstream server. 504 is for an upstream that is too slow to answer.

question.question_text: Why are in-memory server sessions harder to run on two servers than stateless requests?
question.question_html: Why are in-memory server sessions harder to run on two servers than stateless requests?

options.label: A
options.text: Session data sits in one server's memory

options.label: B
options.text: Cookies are bound to a single server IP

options.label: C
options.text: TLS certificates work on one server only

options.label: D
options.text: Browsers keep just one cookie per site

question.explanation: The session exists only on the server that created it, so a request routed to the other server finds no session. A shared store such as Redis fixes this.

question.question_text: A response sends Set-Cookie: token=xyz; SameSite=None with no Secure attribute. What does a modern Chrome browser do?
question.question_html: A response sends Set-Cookie: token=xyz; SameSite=None with no Secure attribute. What does a modern Chrome browser do?

options.label: A
options.text: Stores it and sends it cross-site as asked

options.label: B
options.text: Stores it but treats it as SameSite=Strict

options.label: C
options.text: Stores it only until the browser closes

options.label: D
options.text: Rejects it, since None requires Secure

question.explanation: Browsers reject any cookie with SameSite=None unless Secure is also set, so this cookie is never stored.

question.question_text: In an SSR app that uses hydration, what is true after the HTML arrives but before the JavaScript bundle has run?
question.question_html: In an SSR app that uses hydration, what is true after the HTML arrives but before the JavaScript bundle has run?

options.label: A
options.text: Content shows, but buttons may not respond

options.label: B
options.text: Nothing shows until the bundle has run

options.label: C
options.text: Content and click handlers both fully work

options.label: D
options.text: The server patches the DOM over a socket

question.explanation: The server-rendered HTML is visible as soon as it arrives. Event handlers attach only after the bundle loads and hydrates the page.

question.question_text: A client sends PATCH /accounts/9 with {"balanceIncrement": 100}. The request times out, the client retries, and it turns out the first request had succeeded. What is the result?
question.question_html: A client sends PATCH /accounts/9 with {"balanceIncrement": 100}. The request times out, the client retries, and it turns out the first request had succeeded. What is the result?

options.label: A
options.text: Balance rises by 100, since PATCH is idempotent

options.label: B
options.text: Balance rises by 200, since this PATCH isn't idempotent

options.label: C
options.text: The retry is rejected with 409 automatically

options.label: D
options.text: Balance rises by 100, since HTTP drops duplicates

question.explanation: Applying an increment twice gives a different result, so this PATCH is not idempotent and the retry adds another 100. Idempotency keys prevent this.

question.question_text: A backend engineer designs an endpoint GET [https://api.bank.com/transfer?token=xyz123&amt=500](https://api.bank.com/transfer?token=xyz123&amt=500). Even though HTTPS is enabled, why is passing token=xyz123 in the query string considered a security flaw?
question.question_html: A backend engineer designs an endpoint GET [https://api.bank.com/transfer?token=xyz123&amt=500](https://api.bank.com/transfer?token=xyz123&amt=500). Even though HTTPS is enabled, why is passing token=xyz123 in the query string considered a security flaw?

options.label: A
options.text: HTTPS encrypts the request body, but query parameters travel in plaintext over the network

options.label: B
options.text: Reverse proxies, load balancers, and browser histories routinely log full URLs including query strings

options.label: C
options.text: TLS certificates do not validate query parameters

options.label: D
options.text: Query parameters are cached publicly by default on all CDNs

question.explanation: While HTTPS encrypts the full URL over the network, the server/API gateway decrypts it and standard access logs (Nginx, AWS ALB, CloudWatch) record the request line (path + query) in plaintext, risking credential leaks.

question.question_text: api.shop.com sets a cookie with Domain=shop.com; Path=/account. Which request will the browser send it with?
question.question_html: api.shop.com sets a cookie with Domain=shop.com; Path=/account. Which request will the browser send it with?

options.label: A
options.text: https://shop.com/cart

options.label: B
options.text: https://shop.com/accounts

options.label: C
options.text: https://www.shop.com/account/orders

options.label: D
options.text: https://myshop.com/account

question.explanation: Domain=shop.com covers shop.com and all its subdomains. Path=/account matches /account and /account/... but not /accounts, and myshop.com is a different domain.
